title: A Bayesian Workflow

text:
What “holding Z fixed” means
People say it many ways. They all mean the same thing:

“controlling for Z”
“adjusting for Z”
“conditioning on Z”
“stratifying by Z”

In practice, any of these:

Adding Z to a regression (as we did with height last week).
Splitting the data into groups of Z and comparing within each group.
Selecting your sample by Z: only hospital patients, only published studies, only people with jobs.


That last one is easy to miss. Often the data was “controlled” before you ever saw it.

section: Does marrying later make you happier?
text:
Does marrying later make you happier?

























Overall: people who marry later are happier. Within rural or urban areas: no relationship at all.

The fork: what happened?













Urban people marry later and (in this made-up world) are happier.
Geography is a confounder: a common cause of X and Y.
The path A ← G → H is open: it creates a correlation with no causal effect behind it.
Holding geography fixed closes the path.









Fork rule


Association flows through a fork. Control for the common cause to close the path.

section: Do mobile phones lower birth rates?
text:
Do mobile phones lower birth rates?

























Real World Bank data, 2022. Within income groups the correlation mostly fades (r between -0.31 and -0.06). Wealth drives both phones and smaller families.

You’ve already met forks











Week 2: more bedrooms looked valuable, because bigger houses have more of them.










Week 3: the famous surgeon looked worse, because he got the hardest cases.


The classic Simpson’s paradox, where a trend reverses when you split the data, is usually a fork.

More forks
What’s the hidden common cause?

Ice cream sales ↔︎ drownings → hot weather
Children’s shoe size ↔︎ reading ability → age
Firefighters at a fire ↔︎ damage done → size of the fire
Carrying a lighter ↔︎ lung cancer → smoking
Hospital visits ↔︎ dying → being ill

section: Is there a gender gap in exam results?
text:
Is there a gender gap in exam results?

























A clear gap between groups. But at the same study time, the two lines sit on top of each other: the gap disappears.

The pipe: what happened?













In this made-up world, gender affects results only through study time.
The path G → T → R is open, and it is a real causal effect.
Holding study time fixed closes the path, so the effect vanishes.
Does gender matter? Yes, through study time.









Pipe rule


Association flows through a pipe. Holding the mediator fixed blocks the effect. Only do it if you want the direct effect.

Does the anti-fungal treatment work?






















Overall, treated plants grow more.
Compare plants with the same fungus status and the treatment looks useless.



Post-treatment bias: never hold fixed something the treatment itself changes, unless that’s the question.

A real paradox: Berkeley admissions, 1973













Overall: 45% of men admitted, 30% of women.
But in 4 of 6 departments, women were admitted at a higher rate.
Women mostly applied to the departments that were hardest to get into.
Dot size: number of applicants.

Berkeley: which answer is right?













Department is a pipe: sex affects which department you apply to, and departments differ in how hard they are to get into.
“Do admissions committees treat women differently?” → hold department fixed (the direct path S → A).
“Are women less likely to get in overall?” → don’t (the total effect). Then ask why women ended up applying to the most competitive departments.

Are rich kids lazy?

























Among people with prestigious jobs, the richer ones seem to work less.
But in the whole population (right), wealth and hard work are unrelated.

The collider: what happened?













Wealth or hard work can get you the job.
If someone has the job but isn’t rich, they probably worked hard. If they didn’t work hard, they’re probably rich.
The path W → J ← H is closed by default: no association.
Holding J fixed, including by only looking at people with jobs, opens it.









Collider rule


No association flows through a collider, until you hold it fixed. Don’t control for a common effect, and beware of samples selected on one.

section: Why is published science so often wrong?
text:
Why is published science so often wrong?













200 grant proposals. Newsworthiness and trustworthiness are unrelated.
Reviewers fund the top 10% on both combined.
Among funded studies: r = -0.77.
The most exciting published findings are the least trustworthy, with no bad intent from anyone.
Remember Week 1: most published research findings are false.

More colliders
What has been selected on?

Restaurants in bad locations serve better food → only the good ones survive
Among professional basketball players, height barely predicts success → short players had to be exceptional to make it
Among hospital patients, two unrelated diseases look negatively related → either one can put you in hospital (Berkson’s paradox)
Among low-birth-weight babies, those of smoking mothers die less often → birth weight is caused by smoking and by other, more dangerous problems
Early COVID studies found fewer smokers among hospitalized patients → hospital testing and admission were the collider (Griffith et al., 2020)

Descendants











A proxy for a confounder. We can’t measure wealth exactly, so we used income group. It closes the fork partly, which is why some correlation was left over.










A consequence of a collider. Studying only high earners partly selects on having the job, so it partly opens the collider.

The back-door rule
To estimate the effect of X on Y:

List every path between X and Y.
Close every path that starts with an arrow into X (a “back door”).
Don’t hold fixed anything that X causes (if you want the total effect).
Don’t hold fixed a collider, unless you also close the path it opens.


Last week’s examples follow this rule. Height was caused by sex, so we left it out (rule 3). Living area was a back door into bedrooms, so we held it fixed (rule 2).

A paradox inside a paradox













Back to Berkeley. What if applicants’ ability affects both which department they apply to and whether they get in?
Now department is a pipe and a collider (S → D ← U).
Holding department fixed opens S → D ← U → A, so even the “direct effect” is biased.
No statistical trick fixes this. We need better data (a measure of ability) or more science.

Your turn
For each claim: draw the DAG, name the structure, and decide what to control for.

Students who attend tuition classes score lower on the SEE.
After adjusting for blood pressure, a new drug doesn’t reduce heart attacks.
Among startups that got funding, those with weaker founders had better ideas.
Countries with more doctors per person have more cancer.
People who own more books live longer.
Among people admitted to hospital with COVID, smokers seemed to do better.

Possible answers

Fork: students who are already struggling are the ones sent to tuition. Control for earlier results.
Pipe: the drug works by lowering blood pressure. Don’t adjust if you want the total effect.
Collider: funding needs a strong founder or a strong idea. Don’t trust patterns within a selected sample.
Fork (and a pipe): wealth → more doctors, and wealth → longer lives → more cancer. More doctors also detect more cancer.
Fork: education and income cause both.
Collider: hospitalization. Smoking and severe COVID can each put you there.


There is often more than one defensible DAG. Arguing about which one is right is the science.

Your project

Open your project’s dag in dagitty.net (next slide).
Mark your exposure and outcome.
List every path between them. Label each fork, pipe and collider.
DAGitty’s “Causal effect identification” panel lists the adjustment sets: the variables that close every back door without opening any collider.
Do your model’s variables match? If not, which DAG are you really assuming?

Same data, new ruler























The shape doesn’t change at all. Only the labels on the axis.
The mean becomes 0. The standard deviation becomes 1.
The units disappear: a z-score is measured in “standard deviations”.

In R:

howell |>
  mutate(
    z_height = (height - mean(height)) / sd(height),
    z_weight = (weight - mean(weight)) / sd(weight)
  )



z-scores let us compare things measured on completely different scales: exam marks out of 50 vs. out of 100, rupees vs. dollars, cm vs. kg.
Standardize both variables

Correlation is average agreement


\[
r = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_{\text{height},i} \times z_{\text{weight},i}
\]

Each person “votes”:

Same side of average on both → positive vote
Opposite sides → negative vote

r is the average vote.




cor(howell$height, howell$weight)

[1] 0.7547479




r is always between −1 and +1.
r has no units.
Standardizing changes nothing: r in cm/kg = r in z-scores.

What does r look like?


Our height and weight: r = 0.75. A strong relationship, but far from perfect.

What correlation misses


r only measures straight-line agreement.
Always plot your data before trusting a single number.

The best line













The red lines are the errors: how far each person is from the line.
The best line makes the errors as small as possible overall.
With standardized data and one predictor, the best β is exactly the correlation: β = r = 0.75.

Reading the coefficient



In z-scores: β = 0.75

“An adult 1 SD taller than average is, on average, 0.75 SD heavier.”

Back in real units: β × SDweight / SDheight

0.75 × 6.5 / 7.7 = 0.63 kg per cm
“Each extra centimeter of height goes with about 0.63 kg more weight.”

section: β is a parameter, so it has a distribution
text:
β is a parameter, so it has a distribution


Just like the mayor’s popularity last week: prior × likelihood → posterior.
With 20 people we’re unsure about β. With 352, much less so.

  distinct(`Series Code`, `Series Name`) |>
  filter(!is.na(`Series Code`), !is.na(`Series Name`)) |>
  group_by(`Series Code`) |> # in case of duplicates

  with(setNames(label, `Series Code`))

  select(-c(`Series Name`)) |>
  slice(1:(n() - 5)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^\\d{4} \\[YR\\d{4}\\]$"),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "value",
    names_transform = list(year = ~ str_extract(.x, "^\\d{4}"))
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = `Series Code`, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(across(
    any_of(names(label_vec)),
    ~ {
      attr(.x, "label") <- unname(label_vec[cur_column()])
      .x
    }
  )) |>
  left_join(
    read_csv(filename2),
    join_by(`Country Code` == Code)

plots <- variables |>
  keep(~ .x %in% names(df) && is.numeric(df[[.x]])) |>
  set_names() |>
  map(
    \(v) {
      x_lab <- attr(df[[v]], "label") %||% v

      x_vals <- df[[v]]
      x_vals_non_na <- x_vals[!is.na(x_vals)]

      # Summary stats
      mean_val <- mean(x_vals_non_na)
      sd_val <- sd(x_vals_non_na)

      nepal_value <- df |>
        filter(`Country Name` == "Nepal") |>
        pull(.data[[v]]) |>
        first()

      # Detect whether values are effectively integers
      is_integerish <- length(x_vals_non_na) > 0 &&
        all(abs(x_vals_non_na - round(x_vals_non_na)) < 1e-8)

      # Choose histogram settings automatically
      if (is_integerish && diff(range(x_vals_non_na)) <= 50) {
        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = 1,
          boundary = -0.5,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      } else {
        # Freedman-Diaconis rule for continuous variables
        iqr_val <- IQR(x_vals_non_na)
        n_val <- length(x_vals_non_na)

        fd_binwidth <- 2 * iqr_val / (n_val^(1 / 3))
        fd_binwidth <- 0.5 * fd_binwidth

        # Fallback if IQR is zero or binwidth is not usable
        if (!is.finite(fd_binwidth) || fd_binwidth <= 0) {
          rng <- diff(range(x_vals_non_na))
          fd_binwidth <- if (is.finite(rng) && rng > 0) rng / 30 else 1
        }

        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = fd_binwidth,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      }

      caption_text <- paste0(
        "Mean = ",
        scales::number(mean_val, accuracy = 0.01),
        "   |   SD = ",
        scales::number(sd_val, accuracy = 0.01)
      )

      p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[v]])) +
        hist_geom +
        annotate(

          xmax = mean_val + sd_val,
          ymin = -Inf,
          ymax = Inf,
          fill = "blue",
          alpha = 0.12
        ) +
        geom_vline(
          xintercept = mean_val,
          color = "blue",
          linewidth = 0.9,
          alpha = 0.48
        ) +
        # geom_vline(

        labs(
          title = paste("Histogram of", x_lab),
          x = x_lab,
          y = "Count",
          caption = caption_text
        ) +
        theme_minimal() +
        theme(
          plot.caption = element_text(
            hjust = 0.5,
            margin = margin(t = 8)
          ),
          plot.caption.position = "plot"

plots <- variables |>
  keep(~ .x %in% names(df) && is.numeric(df[[.x]])) |>
  set_names() |>
  map(
    \(v) {
      x_lab <- attr(df[[v]], "label") %||% v

      x_vals <- df[[v]]
      x_vals_non_na <- x_vals[!is.na(x_vals)]

      # Summary stats
      mean_val <- mean(x_vals_non_na)
      sd_val <- sd(x_vals_non_na)

      nepal_value <- df |>
        filter(`Country Name` == "Nepal") |>
        pull(.data[[v]]) |>
        first()

      # Detect whether values are effectively integers
      is_integerish <- length(x_vals_non_na) > 0 &&
        all(abs(x_vals_non_na - round(x_vals_non_na)) < 1e-8)

      # Choose histogram settings automatically
      if (is_integerish && diff(range(x_vals_non_na)) <= 50) {
        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = 1,
          boundary = -0.5,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      } else {
        # Freedman-Diaconis rule for continuous variables
        iqr_val <- IQR(x_vals_non_na)
        n_val <- length(x_vals_non_na)

        fd_binwidth <- 2 * iqr_val / (n_val^(1 / 3))
        fd_binwidth <- 0.5 * fd_binwidth

        # Fallback if IQR is zero or binwidth is not usable
        if (!is.finite(fd_binwidth) || fd_binwidth <= 0) {
          rng <- diff(range(x_vals_non_na))
          fd_binwidth <- if (is.finite(rng) && rng > 0) rng / 30 else 1
        }

        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = fd_binwidth,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      }

      caption_text <- paste0(
        "Mean = ",
        scales::number(mean_val, accuracy = 0.01),
        "   |   SD = ",
        scales::number(sd_val, accuracy = 0.01)
      )

      p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[v]])) +
        hist_geom +
        annotate(
          "rect",
          xmin = mean_val - sd_val,
          xmax = mean_val + sd_val,
          ymin = -Inf,
          ymax = Inf,
          fill = "blue",
          alpha = 0.12
        ) +
        geom_vline(
          xintercept = mean_val,
          color = "blue",
          linewidth = 0.9,
          alpha = 0.48
        ) +
        # geom_vline(
        #   xintercept = c(mean_val - sd_val, mean_val + sd_val),
        #   color = "blue",
        #   linetype = "dashed",
        #   linewidth = 0.8
        # ) +
        labs(
          title = paste("Histogram of", x_lab),
          x = x_lab,
          y = "Count",
          caption = caption_text
        ) +
        theme_minimal() +
        theme(
          plot.caption = element_text(
            hjust = 0.5,
            margin = margin(t = 8)
          ),
          plot.caption.position = "plot"
        )

      if (!is.na(nepal_value)) {
        p <- p +
          geom_vline(
            xintercept = nepal_value,
            color = "red",
            linetype = "dotted",
            linewidth = 0.8
          )
      }

      p
    }
  )

title: Data Lunch
text:
Data Lunch is a short course in applied statistics. It starts from a single uncomfortable claim, that most published research findings are false, and rebuilds statistics so you can tell when a finding deserves to be believed.
The course is Bayesian, in the style of McElreath’s Statistical Rethinking. We think about causes before we touch the data, draw our assumptions as causal diagrams (DAGs), write models in Stan, and check every model on simulated data before trusting it on real data. Students apply each week’s ideas to their own question using World Bank development indicators.

Lectures
Each week is a slide deck. Most weeks have a concepts part and an applied part.



Week
Topic
What you’ll learn




Week 1
A fresh start
Why most published research is false: statistical significance, the base rate paradox, and Bayesian updating.


Week 2
Describing data
Probability distributions, z-scores, correlation, and our first regression coefficient. Applied: what makes a house expensive?


Week 3
Causes and DAGs
Drawing what causes what, what “cause” means in statistics, and the workflow from estimand to estimate. Worked example: does sex affect weight?


Week 4
Confounding
The three building blocks of every DAG (fork, pipe, collider), the paradoxes each one creates, and how to decide what to control for.


Week 5
Acting on evidence
Seven questions to ask of any finding, turning a decision into an estimand, and designing the experiment you wish you could run.





A Bayesian workflow
A Bayesian Workflow is a full worked example that pulls the course together. It asks whether a university’s admissions process discriminates by sex, and goes through eight steps:

Define the estimand.
Draw the causal model (DAG).
Simulate the population.
Write the formal model.
Write the Stan code.
Test on simulated data.
Fit and validate the model.
Compute the estimand and test its robustness.

Along the way it shows Simpson’s paradox: a large overall gap in admission rates that disappears once we compare applicants to the same department.


Homework

Week 1 homework: probability, base rates, and Bayesian updating.



Student projects
Each student picks a question about development outcomes, draws a DAG, and fits a Bayesian regression to the 2022 World Bank data. Nepal is highlighted throughout as the reference case.



Project
Question




Archana
Does access to drinking water services affect water stress?


Ranju
Does corruption affect political stability?


Sambit
Does internet use affect the share of young people not in education, employment or training (NEETs)?


Sameer
Does the length of compulsory education affect vulnerable employment?


Suyash
Does inflation affect GDP growth?


Swasti
Does the share of youth NEETs affect net migration?


Tsering
Does women’s employment affect vulnerable employment?





Reference

World Bank Development Indicators: the variables available for projects, with their codes and coverage.

title: Week 1 Homework
text:
These exercises go with the Week 1 lecture. Part A checks your understanding of the ideas. Parts B–D are problems to work through. Part E is an optional R challenge.
A few ground rules:

Show your work. A correct number with no reasoning is worth less than a wrong number with clear reasoning. Drawing a table of counts (like we did for the HIV example) is almost always the easiest way to do these problems.
Write in plain language. If you can’t explain it to a friend who missed the lecture, you haven’t finished understanding it yet.
Problems marked ★ are harder. Give them a real try, but don’t get stuck on them.


Part A: Concepts
A1. In one or two sentences, explain what probability means in this course. Then explain how a Bayesian and a frequentist would each understand the sentence “The shop near my house is probably open right now.”
A2. Write each of these sentences in probability notation, P( event | condition ):

Of people who smoke, 15% develop lung cancer.
Of people with lung cancer, 85% were smokers.
When Nepal leads at halftime, they win 70% of the time.
40% of students at this university are from Kathmandu.

Statements (a) and (b) are about the same two things, but the numbers are very different. Explain how both can be true at once.
A3. A classmate gets a result with p = 0.03 and says: “So there’s only a 3% chance my hypothesis is wrong.”

Write what a p-value measures in P( … | … ) notation.
Write what your classmate thinks it measures in P( … | … ) notation.
Explain the mistake in your own words.

A4. Match each phrase to its probability statement. (HIV+ means the person has HIV.)

P( test+ | HIV– )


Type I error (false positive)
P( test+ | HIV+ )


Type II error (false negative)
P( test– | HIV– )



Then name the probability that a patient who just tested positive actually cares about. Is it one of the four above?
A5. Ioannidis argued that most published research findings are false, and he did it without re-running a single study. In 4–6 sentences, explain how that is possible. Use the words base rate, power, and false positive in your answer.
A6. True or false? Give a one-sentence reason for each.

A test with 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity gives a correct result 99% of the time for someone who tests positive.
If P(A) = P(B), then P(A | B) = P(B | A).
If your prior probability for a hypothesis is exactly 0, no amount of data can change your mind.
If everything else stays the same, lowering α from 0.05 to 0.005 increases the share of significant results that are true.
If most published findings are false, science doesn’t work.

A7. Find the prior, the likelihood (the observation), and the posterior in each story:

A doctor thinks a patient’s cough is probably a cold. A chest X-ray shows a shadow on the lung, and now the doctor thinks pneumonia is more likely.
You expect the bus to Patan to take about 30 minutes. Three days in a row it takes 50 minutes, so you now leave home earlier.
In lecture: “I think about 60% of Kathmandu will vote for the current mayor… a survey says 30%… I now think about 45%.” Why is the posterior between 60% and 30%, and not exactly 30%? What would push it closer to 30%?



Part B: Probability calculations
B1. In 2025, Kathmandu saw rain on 179 of 365 days. In April it rained on 13 of 30 days, and in July on all 31 days.

What is P( no rain )?
What is P( April | rain )? That is, if you pick a rainy day at random from 2025, how likely is it that the day is in April?
Compare P( rain | April ) with P( April | rain ). Why are they so different?
★ What is P( July | rain )? Why is it nowhere near 1, even though P( rain | July ) = 1?

B3. Make your own 2×2 table from something in your life or work: your village, your office, your cricket team, your WhatsApp groups. Use real counts if you have them, or a reasonable guess if you don’t. Then write one pair of conditional probabilities, P(A | B) and P(B | A), that come out very different, and explain why.


Part C: Base rates
For every problem in this part, build a table of counts for a large population (for example 100,000 people), like the one in lecture.
C1. The HIV test, revisited. Sensitivity is 99%, specificity is 97%, and prevalence is 0.1%.

Rebuild the lecture table and confirm that P( HIV+ | test+ ) ≈ 3.2%.
Now the same test is used in a clinic where 5% of patients have HIV. What is P( HIV+ | test+ ) now?
Go back to 0.1% prevalence, but improve the specificity to 99.9%. What is P( HIV+ | test+ )?
In (b) and (c), which change helped more, and why?
What is P( HIV– | test– ) at 0.1% prevalence? Should someone who tests negative worry?

C2. ★ Testing twice. At 0.1% prevalence, a person tests positive. They take a second, independent test (same sensitivity and specificity) and it also comes back positive. What is the probability they have HIV now? Hint: what is the “prior” for the second test?
C3. AI detectors. A university buys a tool that flags essays as written by AI. It correctly flags 95% of AI-written essays, and wrongly flags 2% of essays that students wrote themselves.

If 10% of submitted essays are AI-written, what share of flagged essays are actually AI-written?
What if only 2% of essays are AI-written?

C4. Ioannidis’s table. In lecture we assumed 1% of tested hypotheses are true, 80% power, and α = 5%. That gave P( true | significant ) ≈ 14%. Using 10,000 tested hypotheses, recompute P( true | significant ) for each case:

Part D: Bayesian updating
These problems use the bag of stones from the lecture app. The bag holds 9 stones, each blue (🔵) or black (⚫️). There are 10 possible bags (0 blue, 1 blue, …, 9 blue), and before drawing we think each one is equally likely. We draw one stone at a time, note its color, and put it back.

Now start from scratch with an equal prior and update on all four draws at once (🔵 ⚫️ 🔵 🔵). Do you get the same answer? Why does this matter?

E1. Write an R function p_true_given_sig(base_rate, power, alpha) that returns P( true | significant ). Use it to check your answers to C4. Then make a plot with base rate (0.001 to 0.5) on the x-axis and P( true | significant ) on the y-axis, with one line for 50% power and one for 80% power.

plots <- variables |>
  keep(~ .x %in% names(df) && is.numeric(df[[.x]])) |>
  set_names() |>
  map(
    \(v) {
      x_lab <- attr(df[[v]], "label") %||% v

      x_vals <- df[[v]]
      x_vals_non_na <- x_vals[!is.na(x_vals)]

      # Summary stats
      mean_val <- mean(x_vals_non_na)
      sd_val <- sd(x_vals_non_na)

      nepal_value <- df |>
        filter(`Country Name` == "Nepal") |>
        pull(.data[[v]]) |>
        first()

      # Detect whether values are effectively integers
      is_integerish <- length(x_vals_non_na) > 0 &&
        all(abs(x_vals_non_na - round(x_vals_non_na)) < 1e-8)

      # Choose histogram settings automatically
      if (is_integerish && diff(range(x_vals_non_na)) <= 50) {
        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = 1,
          boundary = -0.5,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      } else {
        # Freedman-Diaconis rule for continuous variables
        iqr_val <- IQR(x_vals_non_na)
        n_val <- length(x_vals_non_na)

        fd_binwidth <- 2 * iqr_val / (n_val^(1 / 3))
        fd_binwidth <- 0.5 * fd_binwidth

        # Fallback if IQR is zero or binwidth is not usable
        if (!is.finite(fd_binwidth) || fd_binwidth <= 0) {
          rng <- diff(range(x_vals_non_na))
          fd_binwidth <- if (is.finite(rng) && rng > 0) rng / 30 else 1
        }

        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = fd_binwidth,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      }

      caption_text <- paste0(
        "Mean = ",
        scales::number(mean_val, accuracy = 0.01),
        "   |   SD = ",
        scales::number(sd_val, accuracy = 0.01)
      )

      p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[v]])) +
        hist_geom +
        annotate(
          "rect",
          xmin = mean_val - sd_val,
          xmax = mean_val + sd_val,
          ymin = -Inf,
          ymax = Inf,
          fill = "blue",
          alpha = 0.12
        ) +
        geom_vline(
          xintercept = mean_val,
          color = "blue",
          linewidth = 0.9,
          alpha = 0.48
        ) +
        # geom_vline(
        #   xintercept = c(mean_val - sd_val, mean_val + sd_val),
        #   color = "blue",
        #   linetype = "dashed",
        #   linewidth = 0.8
        # ) +
        labs(
          title = paste("Histogram of", x_lab),
          x = x_lab,
          y = "Count",
          caption = caption_text
        ) +
        theme_minimal() +
        theme(
          plot.caption = element_text(
            hjust = 0.5,
            margin = margin(t = 8)
          ),
          plot.caption.position = "plot"
        )

      if (!is.na(nepal_value)) {
        p <- p +
          geom_vline(
            xintercept = nepal_value,
            color = "red",
            linetype = "dotted",
            linewidth = 0.8
          )
      }

      p
    }
  )

plots <- variables |>
  keep(~ .x %in% names(df) && is.numeric(df[[.x]])) |>
  set_names() |>
  map(
    \(v) {
      x_lab <- attr(df[[v]], "label") %||% v

      x_vals <- df[[v]]
      x_vals_non_na <- x_vals[!is.na(x_vals)]

      # Summary stats
      mean_val <- mean(x_vals_non_na)
      sd_val <- sd(x_vals_non_na)

      nepal_value <- df |>
        filter(`Country Name` == "Nepal") |>
        pull(.data[[v]]) |>
        first()

      # Detect whether values are effectively integers
      is_integerish <- length(x_vals_non_na) > 0 &&
        all(abs(x_vals_non_na - round(x_vals_non_na)) < 1e-8)

      # Choose histogram settings automatically
      if (is_integerish && diff(range(x_vals_non_na)) <= 50) {
        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = 1,
          boundary = -0.5,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      } else {
        # Freedman-Diaconis rule for continuous variables
        iqr_val <- IQR(x_vals_non_na)
        n_val <- length(x_vals_non_na)

        fd_binwidth <- 2 * iqr_val / (n_val^(1 / 3))
        fd_binwidth <- 0.5 * fd_binwidth

        # Fallback if IQR is zero or binwidth is not usable
        if (!is.finite(fd_binwidth) || fd_binwidth <= 0) {
          rng <- diff(range(x_vals_non_na))
          fd_binwidth <- if (is.finite(rng) && rng > 0) rng / 30 else 1
        }

        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = fd_binwidth,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      }

      caption_text <- paste0(
        "Mean = ",
        scales::number(mean_val, accuracy = 0.01),
        "   |   SD = ",
        scales::number(sd_val, accuracy = 0.01)
      )

      p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[v]])) +
        hist_geom +
        annotate(

          xmax = mean_val + sd_val,
          ymin = -Inf,
          ymax = Inf,
          fill = "blue",
          alpha = 0.12
        ) +
        geom_vline(
          xintercept = mean_val,
          color = "blue",
          linewidth = 0.9,
          alpha = 0.48

plots <- variables |>
  keep(~ .x %in% names(df) && is.numeric(df[[.x]])) |>
  set_names() |>
  map(
    \(v) {
      x_lab <- attr(df[[v]], "label") %||% v

      x_vals <- df[[v]]
      x_vals_non_na <- x_vals[!is.na(x_vals)]

      # Summary stats
      mean_val <- mean(x_vals_non_na)
      sd_val <- sd(x_vals_non_na)

      nepal_value <- df |>
        filter(`Country Name` == "Nepal") |>
        pull(.data[[v]]) |>
        first()

      # Detect whether values are effectively integers
      is_integerish <- length(x_vals_non_na) > 0 &&
        all(abs(x_vals_non_na - round(x_vals_non_na)) < 1e-8)

      # Choose histogram settings automatically
      if (is_integerish && diff(range(x_vals_non_na)) <= 50) {
        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = 1,
          boundary = -0.5,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      } else {
        # Freedman-Diaconis rule for continuous variables
        iqr_val <- IQR(x_vals_non_na)
        n_val <- length(x_vals_non_na)

        fd_binwidth <- 2 * iqr_val / (n_val^(1 / 3))
        fd_binwidth <- 0.5 * fd_binwidth

        # Fallback if IQR is zero or binwidth is not usable
        if (!is.finite(fd_binwidth) || fd_binwidth <= 0) {
          rng <- diff(range(x_vals_non_na))
          fd_binwidth <- if (is.finite(rng) && rng > 0) rng / 30 else 1
        }

        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = fd_binwidth,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      }

      caption_text <- paste0(
        "Mean = ",
        scales::number(mean_val, accuracy = 0.01),
        "   |   SD = ",
        scales::number(sd_val, accuracy = 0.01)
      )

      p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[v]])) +
        hist_geom +
        annotate(
          "rect",
          xmin = mean_val - sd_val,
          xmax = mean_val + sd_val,
          ymin = -Inf,
          ymax = Inf,
          fill = "blue",
          alpha = 0.12
        ) +
        geom_vline(
          xintercept = mean_val,
          color = "blue",
          linewidth = 0.9,
          alpha = 0.48
        ) +
        # geom_vline(
        #   xintercept = c(mean_val - sd_val, mean_val + sd_val),
        #   color = "blue",
        #   linetype = "dashed",
        #   linewidth = 0.8
        # ) +
        labs(
          title = paste("Histogram of", x_lab),
          x = x_lab,
          y = "Count",
          caption = caption_text
        ) +
        theme_minimal() +
        theme(
          plot.caption = element_text(
            hjust = 0.5,
            margin = margin(t = 8)
          ),
          plot.caption.position = "plot"
        )

      if (!is.na(nepal_value)) {
        p <- p +
          geom_vline(
            xintercept = nepal_value,
            color = "red",
            linetype = "dotted",
            linewidth = 0.8
          )
      }

      p
    }
  )

This, as we can see, an imperfect but reasonably good test.
There’s a problem, though. Can anybody spot it?
If we already know somebody’s HIV status, why would be bother
giving them a test? Far, far more often, when we think about the
accuracy of a test, we are actually interested in the reverse
question:
Sensitivity and Specificity describe a situation where we already
know somebody’s HIV status. Why test if we already know? What we usually
really want a different thing

-Think about that. If you pick a person at random, give them an HIV
test and it comes back positive, there is a 3% chance that they actually
have HIV. 97% of them are getting a positive test (and, likely, quite a
scare) erroneously.

This goes against most people’s expectations. Why this happens
actually isn’t that hard to understand. Of people with HIV, 99% will get
a positive test result.
Of people who don’t have HIV, only 3% will get a positive test
result.
But, the important fact is that HIV is actually quite rare. 3% of
a big population is bigger than 99% of a very small population.
So, this test is 99% accurate at detecting HIV among people who
have it, but for a random person getting a test, a positive test result
is only accurate 3.4% percent of the time.
My point here is not that these tests are worthless. Rather what
I want to point out is that probability is often unpredictable and
unintuitive.

section: So why is most published research wrong?
text:
So why is most published research wrong?
That 14% was the optimistic case. It gets worse when:

the base rate is even lower (genuinely novel ideas are rarer than 1%),
studies are underpowered (real power is often much lower, even 20%),
many comparisons are run, or results are p-hacked (effective α >> 5%).

The problem?


Statistical significance goes against our natural intuitions about uncertainty.
If statistics has ever made you feel dumb or intimidated, it’s not you…
p-value is just a really weird concept.

section: Bayesian Updating: What it is not
text:
Bayesian Updating: What it is not

Statistical Rethinking, p.2 (Richard McElreath, 2020)

Bayesian Updating: What it is
Instead of tests, we have Bayesian Updating:

We have a prior belief about the world (specifically, about a parameter or “estimand”).I think that about 60% of Kathmandu will vote for the current mayor in the next election.
Then, we observe something, and we estimate the likelihood of what we saw given our prior belief.I just took a survey, and only 30% of people said they will vote for the current mayor. This doesn’t really fit with what I expected.
This new observation changes our prior belief (challenging it or making it stronger), to become our posterior.I now think that about 45% of Kathmandu will vote for the current mayor in the next election.


So I said that we were going to derive our entire statistics from
first principles, and I meant it. Instead of a million pre-built tests,
we have one process: Bayesian updating
A million tests. We have one process, called Bayesian updating.
Everything we build will be an application of that same logic.
For those interested in math, I definitely encourage you to where the
theorem comes from and how it’s derived, but for our purposes, we need
just one simple idea:

The Bayesian workflow

Define the estimand: state precisely what you want to know before touching data.
Draw the causal model (DAG): your assumptions about what causes what, from domain knowledge.
Simulate the population: write a generative simulation that could produce data like yours.
Write the formal model: derive the statistical model from the DAG, in mathematical notation.
Write the Stan code: translate the formal model into a program.
Test on simulated data: check that the model recovers known parameters, and that the priors imply plausible data.
Fit and validate the model: run the sampler, check diagnostics (R-hat, ESS, trace plots, divergences), and run posterior predictive checks. Is the model trustworthy?
Compute the estimand and test its robustness: poststratify to get the vote share, then run sensitivity analyses on turnout, poststratification targets, priors, and unmodeled non-response. What is the result, and how much does it depend on our assumptions?

Step 1: The prior


Ask the room to draw their own prior. Someone who remembers the 60%
result from last election might pile weight around 60%. Someone with no
opinion might leave it flat.
The “Score” column is just the height you drew. “Probability”
rescales the scores so they add up to 1. Only the shape
matters.
This prior carries over to the posterior slide, so whatever is drawn
here is what gets updated.


Before seeing any survey, what do you believe about θ? Drag the points.

Step 2: The likelihood


Same question we asked about the HIV test, turned around: for each
possible θ, how likely is the data we saw?
6 of 20 is very plausible if θ is 30%, plausible-ish at 50%,
unlikely at 60%, and almost impossible at 80%.
Point out that the likelihood curve is not a probability
distribution over θ. It’s a set of answers to “P(data | θ)” for many
θs.


We survey 20 voters. 6 of them (30%) say they will vote for the mayor.












How consistent is “6 of 20” with each possible value of θ?

If θ = 30%: P( 6 of 20 ) = 0.192
If θ = 50%: P( 6 of 20 ) = 0.037
If θ = 60%: P( 6 of 20 ) = 0.005
If θ = 80%: P( 6 of 20 ) = 0.0000017


The likelihood is not a belief. It’s what the coin-flip process in the world says about our data, one candidate value of θ at a time.

Step 3: Prior × likelihood → posterior


At each value of θ, multiply the prior’s height by the likelihood’s
height, then rescale so the total is 1. That’s the posterior. Nothing
else is going on.
Start at 20 people and 30%. With a flat prior, the green curve sits
right on the dashed blue one. With a 60% prior, it lands in
between.
Drag the survey size up to a few hundred. The likelihood narrows,
and the prior matters less and less.
“P( mayor wins )” is the share of the posterior above 50%. That’s
the answer people actually want, and it’s the P(hypothesis | data) we
couldn’t get from a significance test.
“Make this posterior my new prior” copies the posterior back onto
the 21 draggable points and clears the survey. Then run a “second poll”.
It’s coarse, since 21 points can’t capture a very narrow curve, but it
shows the idea.

Data gives us seeing. Most of our questions are about doing.
A causal model is the bridge between them.

Step 1: The estimand

“Does sex affect weight?” is too vague to answer.
More precisely:








Estimand


How much heavier, on average, would an adult be if they were male rather than female?





The answer is a number, in kg: the effect of sex on weight.

Step 2: The generative model













Sex affects height (S → H).
Height affects weight (H → W).
Sex might also affect weight directly, e.g. through muscle mass (S → W).
Age affects height and weight (A → H, A → W).
Nothing in this picture causes sex.

section: Step 2: Simulate the world we drew
text:
Step 2: Simulate the world we drew



simulate_people <- function(n) {
  tibble(
    sex = sample(c("female", "male"), n, TRUE),
    male = sex == "male",
    # S -> H: men 10 cm taller
    height = rnorm(n, 150 + 10 * male, 6),
    # H -> W: 0.6 kg per cm
    # S -> W: men 2 kg heavier at the
    #         same height
    weight = rnorm(
      n,
      -45 + 0.6 * height + 2 * male,
      4
    )
  )
}













In this made-up world we know the answers:

Through the direct path alone: 2 kg.
Through both paths: 2 + 0.6 × 10 = 8 kg.

Step 3: Two statistical models


Model A: weight ~ sex
\[
\begin{align}
W_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma) \\
\mu_i &= \alpha_{S[i]} \\
\alpha_j &\sim \text{Normal}(50, 10) \\
\sigma &\sim \text{Normal}^+(0, 10)
\end{align}
\]

Model B: weight ~ sex + height
\[
\begin{align}
W_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma) \\
\mu_i &= \alpha_{S[i]} + \beta H_i \\
\alpha_j &\sim \text{Normal}(50, 10) \\
\beta &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 2) \\
\sigma &\sim \text{Normal}^+(0, 10)
\end{align}
\]


In both, our estimate is the difference: αmale − αfemale.

section: Step 3: Test the models on simulated data
text:
Step 3: Test the models on simulated data


Model A lands near 8 kg. Model B lands near 2 kg.
Each model correctly recovers a different true number. Which one we want depends on the estimand.

Steps 4 & 5: Real data, real estimates


Model A: men are about 6.8 kg heavier.
Model B: at the same height, men are about 0.1 kg heavier. In other words, no difference.

Effects flow through paths











Model A lets the effect flow through both paths: the total effect.










Model B holds height fixed, which blocks the path through height: only the direct effect is left.


Sex affects weight almost entirely through height.
Our estimand asked for the total effect, so Model A answers it. Adding height would hide the very effect we’re asking about.

What about age?













Age is in the DAG, but nothing points from age into sex, so age opens no extra path from sex to weight.
So for this estimand we can leave age out.
Quick check: adding age to the model shifts the sex difference by only 0.25 kg.



Not every variable in the DAG belongs in the model. The DAG tells us which ones do.

Bedrooms: two models


Holding area fixed reverses the sign. An extra bedroom in the same space means smaller rooms.
Here we should hold area fixed: the path through area isn’t the effect we want. With height, we shouldn’t. Same move, opposite advice. The DAG decides.

section: The data can’t draw the DAG for you
text:
The data can’t draw the DAG for you

Many different DAGs fit the same data equally well.
The arrows come from what you know: theory, earlier research, fieldwork, experience, common sense.
If this feels arbitrary: good. You’ve noticed that every conclusion rests on assumptions.
The job isn’t to avoid assumptions. It’s to make them explicit, so other people can argue with them.

A recipe

Name the estimand: “the effect of X on Y”.
List the things that cause Y.
List the things that cause X.
Draw an arrow only where you believe there’s a direct cause. Every missing arrow is a claim.
Include things you can’t measure, too (dashed circles).
Trace every path between X and Y. Which carry the effect you want? Which don’t?

section: Worked example: education and birth rates
text:
Worked example: education and birth rates













World Bank, 2022: 120 countries.
Estimand: the effect of women’s college enrollment on the birth rate.
Countries where more women go to college have fewer births per woman.
But what else is going on?

Two defensible DAGs


DAG 1: development first









Richer countries have more women in college and fewer infant deaths. The red path isn’t an effect of education. Hold infant mortality fixed.

DAG 2: education first









Educated mothers have healthier babies, so families need fewer births. The red path is part of education’s effect. Don’t hold infant mortality fixed.
